beats.say: Here is our puzzle. 8 squared plus 15 squared equals x squared. We must find x.
The little 2 means squared: the number times itself. So 8 squared is 8 times 8, which is 64.
Now 15 squared. What is 15 times 15?

ask.ifNot: Squared means times itself, not times 2. 15 lots of 15 make 225.

beats.say: 15 times 15 is 225.
Add the two squares. 64 plus 225 is 289. So x squared is 289.
Now, which number times itself makes 289? Try 17. 17 times 10 is 170, and 17 times 7 is 119. Together, 289. Yes!
So x is 17.
Careful: x is not 8 plus 15. That gives 23, and 23 times 23 is far more than 289. Square first, then add.
So: square each number, add the squares, then find the number whose square that is.
Here is our puzzle. 5 squared plus 12 squared equals M squared. We must find M.
The little 2 means squared: the number times itself. So 5 squared is 5 times 5, which is 25.
Now 12 squared. What is 12 times 12?

ask.ifNot: Squared means times itself, not times 2. 12 lots of 12 make 144.

beats.say: 12 times 12 is 144.
Add the two squares. 25 plus 144 is 169. So M squared is 169.
Now, which number times itself makes 169? Try 13. 13 times 10 is 130, and 13 times 3 is 39. Together, 169. Yes!
So M is 13.
Careful: 169 is M squared, not M. The question asks for M itself, the number that times itself makes 169.
So: square each number, add the squares, then find the number whose square that is.
The hall has as many rows as there are chairs in each row, and every chair is filled. Which of these could be the number of men?

board.text: Rows = chairs in each row. How many men?

beats.say: Think of a small hall: 5 rows of 5 chairs hold 25 men. So what kind of number is the number of men?

ask.ifNot: Men equals rows times chairs in a row, and those two are the same. So it is a number times itself: a square number.

beats.say: So we are looking for a square number. Let us test each choice against squares we know.
131: 11 times 11 is 121 and 12 times 12 is 144. 131 falls in between, so it is not a square.
275: 16 times 16 is 256 and 17 times 17 is 289. In between again, so not a square.
Now try 18. 18 times 18 is 324. That is one of our choices!
Careful with 325. It is only 1 more than 324, but a full hall needs an exact square. One extra man would have no chair.
So the number of men can be 324.
So: equal rows and columns means a square number. Test each choice by squeezing it between two squares.
4 pairs of numbers. We add each pair, and look for a total that is a square number.

board.text: Which pair adds up to a square number?

beats.say: First pair: 91 plus 19 is 110.
Is 110 a square number? 10 times 10 is 100 and 11 times 11 is 121.

choices: No, it falls between two squares
ask.ifNot: 110 is more than 100 but less than 121. There is no whole number between 10 and 11, so 110 is not a square.

beats.say: 110 sits between 100 and 121, so it is not a square. Next pair: 157 plus 68 is 225.
225 is 15 times 15. A square number!
Let us check the others, to be sure. 59 plus 52 is 111, and 76 plus 78 is 154. Neither is a square.
So the pair is 157 and 68.
A tip: learn the squares of the numbers up to 15 by heart. Then you spot 225 at once.
Which sign goes in the box? We work out the left side, then the right side, and compare.
Left side: 29 times 29. A handy way: 29 times 30 is 870, then take away one 29. That leaves 841.
On the right side, what must we do first?

ask.ifNot: The squares come before the subtraction. So first work out 31 squared and 10 squared, and only then subtract.

beats.say: This is the trap. 31 minus 10 is 21, but we must not subtract first. Each number is squared first.
31 times 31: 31 times 30 is 930, plus one more 31 is 961.
10 squared is 100. So the right side is 961 minus 100, which is 861.
841 is less than 861. So the sign is: less than.
So: squares first, then the take away, then compare.
We must multiply 28 by the smallest number that turns it into a perfect square. The secret is in its prime factors.
Break 28 down. 28 is 2 times 14, and 14 is 2 times 7. So 28 is 2 times 2 times 7.
In a perfect square, every prime factor has a partner. Look at 36: it is 2 times 2 times 3 times 3. Two pairs.
In 28, the two 2s make a pair. Which factor has no partner?

ask.ifNot: 28 is 2 times 2 times 7. The 2s pair up with each other. The 7 stands alone.

beats.say: The 7 is alone. So we give it a partner: multiply by one more 7.
Check: 196 is 14 times 14. A perfect square!
Careful: guessing small numbers does not help here. Any other small number leaves the 7 without a partner.
So: break into primes, pair them up, and multiply by whatever is left alone.
For each pair, we square both numbers and add. We want a total that is itself a square number.

board.text: Sum of the squares of which two is a square?

beats.say: Start with 10 and 15. 10 squared is 100 and 15 squared is 225. Together, 325.
Is 325 a square? 18 times 18 is 324. So 325 misses by just 1. Not a square.
Next, 7 and 24. 7 squared is 49. For 24 squared: 24 times 20 is 480 and 24 times 4 is 96. So what is 24 times 24?

ask.ifNot: Add the two parts. 480 plus 96 makes 576.

beats.say: 480 plus 96 is 576. So the total is 49 plus 576, which is 625.
And 625 is 25 times 25. A square!
The other two pairs give 2089 and 706, and neither of those is a square.
So the pair is 7 and 24.
The trap is the first pair. 325 is so close to 324 that it is easy to believe. Close is not enough for a square.
We must multiply 588 by the least number that makes a perfect square. The secret is in its prime factors.
Break 588 down. 588 is 2 times 294, and 294 is 2 times 147.
147 is 3 times 49, and 49 is 7 times 7. So 588 is 2 times 2 times 3 times 7 times 7.
In a perfect square every factor has a partner. The 2s make a pair and the 7s make a pair. Which factor is alone?

ask.ifNot: There are two 2s and two 7s, so they pair up. There is only one 3, so it is alone.

beats.say: The 3 is alone. So we multiply by 3 to give it a partner.
Check: 1764 is 42 times 42. A perfect square.
So the least number is 3. Now look at the choices: 2, 6 and 4. There is no 3!
Here is the trap. When your answer is not in the list, do not bend it to fit. The answer is None of these.
A quick check of the others: multiplying by 2, 4 or 6 still leaves a factor without a partner.
We add something to 1234 to reach a square number. So we need the first square above 1234.

spec.note: How far is the next square?

beats.say: Where to start? 30 times 30 is 900, too small. 40 times 40 is 1600, too big. So try in between, at 35.
35 times 35 is 1225. That is just under 1234.
1225 is below 1234. So which square should we aim for?

ask.ifNot: We are adding, so we must go up. The next square after 35 times 35 is 36 times 36.

beats.say: 36 times 36: 36 times 30 is 1080, and 36 times 6 is 216. Together, 1296.
Now find the gap from 1234 up to 1296. It is 62.
So we must add 62.
Check: 1234 plus 62 is 1296, and that is 36 times 36.
3 pairs of numbers. We add each pair, and look for a total that is a square number.

board.text: Which two numbers add up to a square?

beats.say: First pair: 159 plus 165 is 324.
Is 324 a square? Try 18. 18 times 10 is 180, and 18 times 8 is 144. So what is 18 times 18?

ask.ifNot: 18 times 18 is 18 times 10 and 18 times 8 together. 180 plus 144 makes 324.

beats.say: 180 plus 144 is 324. So 324 is 18 times 18, a square!
Check the others. 198 plus 145 is 343. That is past 324, but short of 19 times 19, which is 361. Not a square.
189 plus 330 is 519. 22 times 22 is 484 and 23 times 23 is 529. In between, so not a square.
So the pair is 159 and 165.
Careful: do not jump to none of these because the sums look hard. Add each pair properly first.
Two special squares to find, and then we divide one by the other.
The smallest 4-digit number is 1000. 30 times 30 is 900, so we are close. 31 times 31 is 961. Still only 3 digits.
Try 32. 32 times 32 is 1024. That is the smallest 4-digit square.
Now the 2-digit squares: 16, 25, 36, 49, 64 and 81. Which is the greatest even one?

ask.ifNot: 81 is the greatest, but it is odd. The greatest even one is 64.

beats.say: 81 is bigger, but it is odd. That is the trap. The greatest even one is 64.
Now divide 1024 by 64. 64 times 10 is 640. That leaves 384, and 64 times 6 is 384.
10 lots and 6 lots make 16 lots. So the quotient is 16.
So: find each special number carefully, word by word, and only then divide.
We divide the greatest 2-digit square by the smallest 2-digit square, and find what is left over.
List the squares. 1, 4 and 9 have one digit. Then come 16, 25, 36, 49, 64 and 81. And 100 has 3 digits.
So the greatest 2-digit square is 81 and the smallest is 16.
Now divide 81 by 16. 5 times 16 is 80 and 6 times 16 is 96. So how many lots of 16 fit into 81?

ask.ifNot: 5 lots make 80, which fits inside 81. 6 lots make 96, which is too much.

beats.say: 5 lots of 16 make 80. 6 lots would be 96, which is too many.
81 minus 80 leaves 1. That is the remainder.
Check: 5 times 16, plus 1, is 81.
Careful: 100 is a square, but it has 3 digits. The greatest 2-digit square is 81.
6 numbers, and one does not belong. First, what do they all have in common?
What kind of numbers are these?

ask.ifNot: 144 is 12 times 12. In the same way, every number here is some number times itself, so they are square numbers.

beats.say: They are all squares: of 12, 13, 14, 16, 18 and 20.
So being a square does not pick one out. Look again at the numbers being squared: 12, 13, 14, 16, 18 and 20.
All of them are even, except 13. And an odd number squared stays odd. 169 is the only odd number in the list.
So the odd one out is 169.
When everything looks alike, dig one level deeper. Here, that meant asking what each number is the square of.
6 numbers, and one does not belong. They are all square numbers, so let us find what each is the square of.
81 is 9 times 9. 121 is 11 times 11. 169 is 13 times 13.
289 is 17 times 17. 361 is 19 times 19. And 529 is 23 times 23.
Look at 9, 11, 13, 17, 19 and 23. What is special about most of them?

ask.ifNot: 11, 13, 17, 19 and 23 can only be divided by 1 and themselves. They are prime numbers.

beats.say: 5 of them are prime. But 9 is not prime, because 9 is 3 times 3.
So 81 is the square of a number that is not prime. It does not belong.
The trap: all 6 numbers are odd, and all are squares, so those ideas do not help. The difference hides in the number being squared.
The square of 12 means 12 multiplied by itself.
Which sum gives the square of 12?

ask.ifNot: Squaring means the number times itself. So it is 12 times 12, not 12 times 2.

beats.say: 12 times 12 is easier in two parts. Split one 12 into 10 and 2.
12 times 10 is 120. And 12 times 2 is 24.
120 plus 24 is 144. So the square of 12 is 144.
Careful: 10 times 10 plus 2 times 2 is only 104. That leaves out part of the square.
So remember: the square of a number is the number times itself.
A perfect square is a number times itself, like 3 times 3. One of these 4 numbers is a perfect square.
List the squares near these numbers. 6 times 6 is 36. 7 times 7 is 49. 8 times 8 is 64. 9 times 9 is 81.
Which of our numbers is in that list of squares?

ask.ifNot: Look down the list of squares: 36, 49, 64, 81. Only 64 is one of our numbers.

beats.say: 64 is 8 times 8. So 64 is the perfect square.
Careful: 48, 56 and 72 are in the times tables too. But 48 is 6 times 8, and 56 is 7 times 8. Two different numbers.
A perfect square needs the same number twice.
The board has 81 small squares, with as many rows as columns. How many squares are in each row?

board.text: 81 small squares, equal rows and columns. Each row = ?

beats.say: Rows and columns are equal. So the number in a row, times what, makes 81?

ask.ifNot: There are as many rows as squares in a row. So we multiply the number by itself to get 81.

beats.say: We need a number that, times itself, makes 81.
Try 8. 8 times 8 is 64. Too small.
Try 9. 9 times 9 is 81. That fits! So each row has 9 small squares.
Careful: do not divide 81 by 3, and do not halve it. The board is square, so both numbers must be the same.
We know only one thing about a number: it ends in 7. Can we still tell how its square ends?

board.text: A number ends in 7. Its square ends in ?

beats.say: Test with the simplest such number, 7 itself. 7 times 7 is 49, which ends in 9.
Will a bigger number that ends in 7, like 17, also have a square ending in 9?

choices: Yes, only the last digits matter
No, it could end in anything
ask.ifNot: When we multiply, the last digit of the answer comes only from the last digits of the two numbers. Here that is 7 times 7.

beats.say: 17 times 17: 17 times 10 is 170 and 17 times 7 is 119. Together, 289. It ends in 9 again!
The last digit of a product comes only from the last digits. And 7 times 7 always ends in 9.
Careful: the last digit does not just stay 7. And 7 plus 7 is 14, but squaring is multiplying, not adding.
49 is a perfect square, and we want the very next one after it.
49 is which number times itself?

ask.ifNot: 7 times 7 is 49. So 49 is the square of 7.

beats.say: 49 is 7 times 7.
The next square comes from the next counting number, which is 8.
8 times 8 is 64. So the next perfect square is 64.
Careful: 56 is 7 times 8. For the next square, both numbers must go up to 8.
The squares go 49, 64, then 81. There is no perfect square in between.
Ravi plants 11 rows of saplings, with 11 saplings in each row. How many saplings is that?
Which sum counts all the saplings?

ask.ifNot: Each row has 11, and there are 11 rows. So we add 11, eleven times over. That is 11 times 11.

beats.say: 11 times 11. Start with 11 times 10, which is 110.
Then one more 11. 110 plus 11 is 121.
So Ravi plants 121 saplings.
Careful: 22 is only 11 plus 11, which is just 2 rows. And 44 counts along the 4 sides. The saplings fill the whole field.
5 squared plus 3 squared. The little 2 tells us to square each number.
What does 5 squared mean?

ask.ifNot: The little 2 means: use the number twice in a multiplication. So 5 squared is 5 times 5.

beats.say: 5 squared is 5 times 5, which is 25.
3 squared is 3 times 3, which is 9.
Now add the two squares. 25 plus 9 is 34.
Careful: do not add first. 5 plus 3 is 8, and 8 squared is 64. That is a different sum.
So: square each number on its own, then add.
The square of 30 is 30 times 30.
Here is a trick for numbers that end in zero. First forget the zeros: 3 times 3 is 9.
Now put the zeros back. Each 30 has one zero. How many zeros go on the answer?

ask.ifNot: One zero comes from the first 30 and one from the second 30. That makes 2 zeros.

beats.say: One zero from each 30 makes 2 zeros. So we write 9, and then 2 zeros. That is 900.
Check: 30 times 10 is 300, and 3 lots of 300 make 900.
Careful: 60 is 30 plus 30. And 90 has only one zero. The square needs both zeros.
We want the biggest perfect square that still has only two digits.
The greatest two-digit number is 99. So we want the biggest square that is not more than 99.
10 times 10 is 100. Is that a two-digit number?

ask.ifNot: 100 has 3 digits: 1, 0 and 0. So it is too big for us.

beats.say: 100 is too big. Step back one: 9 times 9 is 81.
81 has two digits. So 81 is the greatest two-digit perfect square.
Careful: 99 is the greatest two-digit number, but no whole number times itself makes 99. It lies between 81 and 100.
We take away as little as we can from 30, and we must be left with a perfect square.
We are taking away, so the square we want is below 30. And for the smallest take away, it should be as near to 30 as possible.
5 times 5 is 25 and 6 times 6 is 36. Which of these can we reach by taking away from 30?

ask.ifNot: 36 is more than 30. We are taking away, so we need the square that is less than 30, which is 25.

beats.say: 25 is the nearest square below 30.
30 minus 25 is 5. So we take away 5.
Careful: 6 is what you would add to reach 36. And taking away 14 or 21 also leaves a square, but they are not the smallest.
So: the smallest take away leads to the nearest square below.
All 4 of these are perfect squares. We want the one that is the square of an odd number.

board.text: Which is the square of an odd number?

beats.say: Find what each one is the square of. 36 is 6 times 6. 64 is 8 times 8. 100 is 10 times 10.
6, 8 and 10 are all even. So those three are squares of even numbers.
49 is 7 times 7. Is 7 odd or even?

ask.ifNot: Even numbers end in 0, 2, 4, 6 or 8. 7 is not one of those, so 7 is odd.

beats.say: 7 is odd. So 49 is the square of an odd number.
A shortcut: odd times odd is always odd. So the square of an odd number must be odd, and 49 is the only odd number here.
Two steps here: find the square of 6, and then compare it with 6 itself.
First, the square of 6. What is it?

ask.ifNot: The square of 6 is 6 times 6, which is 36. 6 times 2 would only be 12.

beats.say: 6 times 6 is 36.
Difference means subtract. So take the number 6 away from its square. 36 minus 6 is 30.
Picture it: from 6 rows of 6, take away one row. 5 rows of 6 are left, and that is 30.
Careful: 36 is only the square. The question has one more step. And difference never means add.
We count the perfect squares that lie between 50 and 150.

board.text: How many perfect squares between 50 and 150?

beats.say: Find where to start. 7 times 7 is 49, just below 50. So the first square inside is 8 times 8, which is 64.
Carry on. 9 times 9 is 81, 10 times 10 is 100, 11 times 11 is 121 and 12 times 12 is 144.
13 times 13 is 169. Does that one count?

ask.ifNot: 169 is bigger than 150, so it is outside our range. We stop at 144.

beats.say: So the squares are 64, 81, 100, 121 and 144.
Count them. There are 5 perfect squares.
Careful at both ends. 49 is just outside, and so is 169. Always check the edges.
One of these digits can never be the last digit of a perfect square. Let us find out which.

board.text: Which digit is never the last digit of a perfect square?

beats.say: The last digit of a square depends only on the last digit of the number. So we just square the digits 0 to 9.
Their last digits are 0, 1, 4, 9, 6, 5, 6, 9, 4 and 1.
Which of our 4 digits is missing from that list?

ask.ifNot: 4 is there, from 2 times 2. 5 is there, from 5 times 5. 6 is there, from 4 times 4. But 7 never appears.

beats.say: 7 never shows up. So no perfect square ends in 7.
In fact squares only ever end in 0, 1, 4, 5, 6 or 9. Never in 2, 3, 7 or 8. A handy fact for spotting squares!
10 squared, take away 6 squared. We square each number first.
10 squared is 10 times 10, which is 100.
And what is 6 squared?

ask.ifNot: 6 squared is 6 times 6, which is 36. 6 times 2 would be only 12.

beats.say: 6 squared is 36.
Now subtract. 100 minus 36 is 64.
Careful: do not subtract first. 10 minus 6 is 4, and 4 squared is only 16.
So: squares first, then the take away.
We add up these 6 odd numbers, and then ask which number the total is the square of.
A neat way to add: pair the ends. 1 and 11 make 12. 3 and 9 make 12. 5 and 7 make 12.
3 lots of 12 make 36.
The total is 36. Which number, times itself, makes 36?

ask.ifNot: 6 times 6 is 36. The question asks for the number that is squared, not for the total.

beats.say: 6 times 6 is 36. So the sum is the square of 6.
Here is the pretty part. We added 6 odd numbers, and got 6 times 6. That always works!

spec.note: 6 odd numbers build a 6 by 6 square

beats.say: Try it: 1 plus 3 is 4, which is 2 times 2. And 1 plus 3 plus 5 is 9, which is 3 times 3.
The teacher makes the biggest square she can from 150 children. Some will not fit. How many?

board.text: 150 children, biggest possible square. Left out = ?

beats.say: A square has the same number in every row and column. So the number she uses is a perfect square, as big as possible, but not more than 150.
12 times 12 is 144. And 13 times 13 is 169.
Which square can the teacher make with 150 children?

ask.ifNot: 13 by 13 needs 169 children, but there are only 150. So the biggest square she can make is 12 by 12.

beats.say: 169 is too many. So the biggest square uses 144 children.
The rest are left out. 150 minus 144 is 6.
Careful: 12 is the number in each row, not the number left out. And 19 is how many more she would need for the next square.
The gardener wants to plant all 200 roses in a square. He may need to buy a few more. How many, at least?

board.text: 200 plants, all in a square. Extra plants needed = ?

beats.say: He wants to use every plant, so the square must hold at least 200. We need the first perfect square that is 200 or more.
14 times 14 is 196. Can a 14 by 14 square hold all 200 plants?

ask.ifNot: 196 is 4 short of 200. So 4 plants would be left over, and he wants to plant them all.

beats.say: 196 is too small. This is the trap: we must go up to the next square, not down.
15 times 15 is 225. That holds them all.
He has 200 and needs 225. 225 minus 200 is 25. So he buys 25 more.
Careful: 4 is how many would be left over from the smaller square. And 15 is the number in each row, not the number to buy.
The square root of 400, added to the square root of 49. We find each root first, and then add.
The square root of 400 is the number that, times itself, makes 400. Which is it?

ask.ifNot: 20 times 20 is 400, because 2 times 2 is 4, with 2 zeros. 200 is only half of 400, and a square root is not a half.

beats.say: 20 times 20 is 400. So the square root of 400 is 20.
7 times 7 is 49. So the square root of 49 is 7.
Now add. 20 plus 7 is 27.
Careful: do not add first. 400 plus 49 is 449, and that is not what the question asks.
So: find each square root on its own, then add.
441 soldiers stand in a square, and every soldier in the front row holds a flag. How many flags?

board.text: 441 soldiers in a square. Flags in the front row = ?

beats.say: We need the number of soldiers in one row. That number, times itself, is 441.
Try 20. 20 times 20 is 400. A bit too small.
400 is too small. Here is a clue: 441 ends in 1. Which number should we try next?

ask.ifNot: We need just a little more than 20. And 21 ends in 1, so its square ends in 1 too, like 441.

beats.say: 21 times 21: 21 times 20 is 420, and one more 21 makes 441.
So each row has 21 soldiers, and the front row holds 21 flags.
Careful: only the front row holds flags. Not all four sides, and not all 441 soldiers.
Three of these are perfect squares, and one is not. We want the one that is not.

board.text: Which is NOT a perfect square?

beats.say: List the squares just above 10 times 10. 11 times 11 is 121. 12 times 12 is 144.
13 times 13 is 169. 14 times 14 is 196.
Which of our numbers is missing from the list 121, 144, 169, 196?

ask.ifNot: 121, 144 and 196 are all in the list of squares. 164 is not there.

beats.say: 164 is not in the list. It sits between 144 and 169, so it is not a perfect square.
Careful: 164 looks a lot like 169 and 144. Looking like a square is not enough. Check against the tables.
Two numbers come one after the other. Their squares are 144 and 169. We want the sum of the two numbers.

board.text: Squares are 144 and 169. Sum of the two numbers = ?

beats.say: 144 is the square of which number?

ask.ifNot: 12 times 12 is 144. 72 is half of 144, and a square root is not a half.

beats.say: 12 times 12 is 144. So the first number is 12.
The numbers come one after the other, so the second should be 13. Check: 13 times 13 is 169. Yes!
Now add the two numbers. 12 plus 13 is 25.
Careful: the question asks for the sum of the numbers, not of their squares. 144 plus 169 is 313, a very different answer.
Only one of these 4 numbers is a perfect square. We can find it without any long multiplying, just from the last digits.

board.text: Only one is a perfect square. Use the last digits.

beats.say: Remember how squares end. Square the digits 0 to 9, and the last digits are only ever 0, 1, 4, 5, 6 or 9.
So which endings are impossible for a perfect square?

ask.ifNot: Squares can end in 0, 1, 4, 5, 6 or 9. The digits left over are 2, 3, 7 and 8, and no square ends in those.

beats.say: 1232 ends in 2. 1443 ends in 3. 1687 ends in 7. All three are ruled out.
Only 1521 is left. It ends in 1, which is fine.
And indeed, 39 times 39 is 1521.
Careful: a good ending does not prove a number is a square. But a bad ending proves it is not. That was enough here.
4 squares to add. We square each number first, and then add them up.
1 times 1 is 1. And 2 times 2 is 4.
What is 3 squared?

ask.ifNot: 3 squared is 3 times 3, which is 9. 3 times 2 would be 6, but squaring is times itself.

beats.say: 3 times 3 is 9. And 4 times 4 is 16.
Now add the squares. 1 plus 4 plus 9 plus 16 is 30.
Careful: adding first gives 1 plus 2 plus 3 plus 4, which is 10, and 10 squared is 100. Not the same thing at all.
Tara has a square made of 64 tiles. She wants to grow it into the next bigger square. How many more tiles?

board.text: 64 tiles in a square. Tiles for the next bigger square?

beats.say: 64 tiles make a square. How many tiles are along each side?

ask.ifNot: We need a number that, times itself, makes 64. 8 times 8 is 64, so each side has 8 tiles.

beats.say: 8 times 8 is 64. So her square is 8 by 8.
The next bigger square is 9 by 9. And 9 times 9 is 81.
She has 64 and needs 81. 81 minus 64 is 17.
See where the 17 tiles go: one new row of 8, one new column of 8, and 1 tile in the corner.
That corner tile is the trap. Forget it, and you get 16.
A number, squared, makes 225. We take the number that is 1 more, and square that instead.

board.text: A number squared is 225. (The number + 1) squared = ?

beats.say: Which number, times itself, makes 225? A clue: 10 times 10 is 100 and 20 times 20 is 400.

ask.ifNot: 225 is between 100 and 400, so the number is between 10 and 20. And 225 ends in 5, so the number ends in 5. That is 15.

beats.say: 15 times 15 is 225. So the number is 15.
One more than 15 is 16.
16 times 16: 16 times 10 is 160, and 16 times 6 is 96. Together, 256.
Careful: add 1 to the number, not to its square. 225 plus 1 is 226, and that is not a square at all.
So: go back to the number, change it, and then square again.
We count every perfect square from 1 to 100, with both ends included.

board.text: How many perfect squares from 1 to 100?

beats.say: The first one is 1 times 1, which is 1. Yes, 1 is a perfect square!
And the last one? Which number, times itself, makes exactly 100?

ask.ifNot: 10 times 10 is 100. So 100 is itself a perfect square, the square of 10.

beats.say: 10 times 10 is 100. So the squares run from the square of 1 up to the square of 10.
Here they all are.
Each number from 1 to 10 gives one square. So there are 10 of them.
Careful: both ends count here, 1 and 100. Miss one and you get 9. And 11 times 11 is 121, which is too big.
51 squared, take away 49 squared. Big numbers, but there is a neat way in.
Start with 51 times 50, which is 2550.
51 times 51 is one more 51 than that. 2550 plus 51 is 2601.
Now 49 times 49. 49 times 50 is 2450. Is 49 times 49 more or less than that?

ask.ifNot: 49 times 49 has one 49 fewer than 49 times 50. So we take 49 away.

beats.say: Now subtract the squares. 2601 minus 2401 is 200.
The trap: 51 minus 49 is 2, and 2 squared is 4. But we must square first, and only then subtract.
A shortcut to enjoy: add the two numbers to get 100, and multiply by their difference, 2. That gives 200 as well.
We divide 48 by something, and the result must be a perfect square. We want the smallest number that works.
Smallest means we test small numbers in order. Dividing by 1 leaves 48, which is not a square.
Divide by 2 and we get 24. Is 24 a square? 4 times 4 is 16 and 5 times 5 is 25. So no.
Now divide by 3. What is 48 divided by 3?

ask.ifNot: 3 times 16 is 48. So 48 divided by 3 is 16.

beats.say: 48 divided by 3 is 16. And 16 is 4 times 4. A perfect square!
So the smallest number to divide by is 3.
Careful: dividing by 12 gives 4, which is a square too. But 12 is not the smallest. That is why we test in order.
We subtract as little as we can from 1000, and we must land on a perfect square.
We need the biggest perfect square below 1000. 30 times 30 is 900. So try the numbers just above 30.
31 times 31: 31 times 30 is 930, and one more 31 makes 961.
32 times 32 is 1024. Can we use that one?

ask.ifNot: We are subtracting from 1000, so the square must be less than 1000. 1024 is above it.

beats.say: 1024 is above 1000. This is the trap: it is nearer, but we cannot reach it by taking away. So our square is 961.
1000 minus 961 is 39.
Check: 1000 minus 39 is 961, which is 31 times 31.
Careful: 31 is the number we squared, not the number to subtract.
We count the whole numbers that lie between 15 squared and 16 squared.

board.text: How many whole numbers between 15² and 16²?

beats.say: First work out the two squares. 15 times 15 is 225, and 16 times 16 is 256.
The numbers between them start at 226 and end at 255.
256 minus 225 is 31. Is that the number of whole numbers in between?

ask.ifNot: The gap of 31 counts every step from 225 up to 256, and the last step lands on 256 itself. So there is one fewer in between.

beats.say: This is the trap. There are 31 steps, but the last step lands on 256, which is an end. So 30 numbers are in between.
Check another way: from 226 to 255 is 255 minus 226, plus 1.
A pattern: between 15 squared and 16 squared there are 2 times 15 numbers. It works for any two neighbours.
The farmer has enough trees for one square, with 5 left over. For the next bigger square he is 20 short. How many trees has he?

board.text: A square with 5 left over; 20 more for the next square

beats.say: Picture his trees on a number line. He is 5 past one perfect square, and 20 short of the next one.
So how far apart are those two squares?

ask.ifNot: From the smaller square up to his trees is 5. From his trees up to the bigger square is 20. Together that is 5 plus 20.

beats.say: 5 plus 20 is 25. We need two neighbouring squares that are 25 apart.
A tip: neighbouring squares differ by the sum of the two numbers. 12 plus 13 is 25, so try 12 and 13.
12 times 12 is 144, and 13 times 13 is 169. And yes, 169 minus 144 is 25!
So his square holds 144 trees, with 5 left over. 144 plus 5 is 149.
Check: 149 plus 20 is 169, the next square. And careful: 144 forgets the 5 left over.
Asha has two square sheets of stamps: 9 rows of 9, and 12 rows of 12. She makes one big square from all of them.

board.text: 9 rows of 9 and 12 rows of 12, made into one square

beats.say: Count the stamps on each sheet. 9 times 9 is 81. And 12 times 12 is 144.
Altogether, 81 plus 144 is 225 stamps.
The big square has 225 stamps. How do we find the number in each row?

ask.ifNot: In a square, the rows and columns are equal. So we need the number that, times itself, makes 225.

beats.say: Try 15. 15 times 10 is 150, and 15 times 5 is 75. Together, 225.
So the big square has 15 stamps in each row.
The trap: 9 plus 12 is 21, but sides cannot simply be added. 21 times 21 is 441, far more stamps than she has.
A riddle with two clues. I am a two-digit perfect square, and my digits add up to 13.

board.text: A two-digit perfect square. Its digits add up to 13.

beats.say: Start with the stronger clue: a two-digit perfect square. There are only 6 of those.
Now test the second clue on each. 1 plus 6 is 7. 2 plus 5 is 7. 3 plus 6 is 9. None of those is 13.
What do the digits of 49 add up to?

ask.ifNot: The digits of 49 are 4 and 9. And 4 plus 9 is 13.

beats.say: 4 plus 9 is 13. That fits!
The last two: 6 plus 4 is 10, and 8 plus 1 is 9. So only 49 works.
Careful: 67 and 94 also have digits that add up to 13. But they are not perfect squares. Both clues must fit.
We want the smallest perfect square that can be divided exactly by 6, and also by 8.

board.text: Smallest perfect square that 6 and 8 both divide

beats.say: It can be divided by 8, so it must be even. So we only test the even squares, in order.
4 and 16 cannot be divided by 6. 36 can, but 36 cannot be divided exactly by 8.
64 is 8 times 8, so 8 divides it. Does 6 divide 64 exactly?

ask.ifNot: 6 times 10 is 60 and 6 times 11 is 66. 64 falls between them, so 6 does not divide it exactly.

beats.say: 64 is out. And 100 is out too, because 6 times 16 is 96 and 6 times 17 is 102.
Now 144. 144 divided by 6 is 24, and 144 divided by 8 is 18. Both are exact!
So the smallest such perfect square is 144.
The trap is 24 or 48. Both 6 and 8 divide them, but they are not perfect squares. Every word of the question counts.
Most numbers have an even number of factors. We count the numbers from 1 to 50 that have an odd number of factors.

board.text: 1 to 50: how many numbers have an odd number of factors?

beats.say: Factors come in pairs. For 12: 1 and 12, 2 and 6, 3 and 4. That is 3 pairs, so 6 factors. An even count.
Now look at 16: 1 and 16, 2 and 8, and then 4 and 4.
4 and 4 is a pair made of the same number. How many times do we count the factor 4?

ask.ifNot: 4 is just one factor of 16. We do not list it twice. So this pair adds only 1 to the count.

beats.say: So 16 has 5 factors: 1, 2, 4, 8 and 16. An odd count! That happens when a factor pairs with itself.
This is the key idea. A number has an odd number of factors only when it is a perfect square.
So we just count the perfect squares up to 50.
There are 7. The next square, 64, is past 50.
Careful: this is not about odd numbers, and not about prime numbers. It is about squares.
A pattern is given, and we use it to add all the odd numbers from 1 to 39. No long adding needed!
Look at the answers: 4, 9, 16. Those are 2 times 2, 3 times 3 and 4 times 4. All squares!
1 plus 3 plus 5 has 3 numbers, and its sum is 3 times 3. So what gets squared?

ask.ifNot: With 3 odd numbers the sum is 3 times 3. With 4 odd numbers it is 4 times 4. So we square how many numbers there are.

beats.say: The sum is the count of odd numbers, times itself. So we need to know how many odd numbers there are from 1 to 39.
From 1 to 40 there are 40 numbers, and half of them are odd. Half of 40 is 20.
So there are 20 odd numbers, and the sum is 20 times 20, which is 400.
The trap is to square the last number, 39. The pattern squares the count, not the last number.
Check with the pattern: 1, 3, 5, 7 ends in 7, and half of 7 plus 1 is 4. The sum was 4 times 4. It fits.
Two numbers come one after the other, and their squares differ by 37. We want the larger number.

board.text: Two neighbours. Their squares differ by 37. Larger = ?

beats.say: Look for a pattern with small neighbours first. 4 squared is 16 and 5 squared is 25. The difference is 9.
The squares of 4 and 5 differ by 9. How is 9 connected to 4 and 5?

ask.ifNot: 4 plus 5 is 9. The difference of two neighbouring squares is the sum of the two numbers.

beats.say: 4 plus 5 is 9. Try another pair, 5 and 6. 36 minus 25 is 11, and 5 plus 6 is 11. It works again!
So our two neighbours add up to 37. Which neighbours add up to 37? 18 and 19.
Check with the squares. 19 times 19 is 361 and 18 times 18 is 324. They differ by 37.
So the larger number is 19.
Careful: 18 is the smaller one. And 37 is the gap between the squares, not one of the numbers.
144 children stand in a square. Only the children on the outside edge hold a flag. How many is that?

board.text: 144 children in a square. How many on the outside edge?

beats.say: First, the size of the square. 12 times 12 is 144, so each side has 12 children.
There are 4 sides with 12 children on each. Is the answer 4 times 12, which is 48?

choices: No, the corners get counted twice
ask.ifNot: A child in a corner stands on two sides at once. So 4 times 12 counts each corner child twice.

beats.say: This is the trap. Each corner child belongs to two sides, so 48 counts 4 children twice.
Take away those 4 extra counts. 48 minus 4 is 44.
Check another way. The top and bottom rows have 12 each. The two sides have 10 more each, without the corners.
Or think of the children inside: they make a 10 by 10 square of 100. And 144 minus 100 is 44.
A square floor of 225 tiles. The tiles on both diagonals are red. How many red tiles?

board.text: 225 tiles in a square. Both diagonals are red. How many?

beats.say: First the size. 15 times 15 is 225, so the floor is 15 tiles by 15 tiles.
A diagonal goes from corner to corner, and takes one tile from every row. So each diagonal has 15 tiles.
Two diagonals of 15 tiles. Is the answer 15 plus 15, which is 30?

choices: No, they share the middle tile
ask.ifNot: 15 is odd, so there is one tile exactly in the middle. Both diagonals pass through it, and 30 counts it twice.

beats.say: Here is the trap. Because 15 is odd, the two diagonals cross on the middle tile. We counted that tile twice.
So take 1 away. 30 minus 1 is 29.
Look at the small floor, 5 by 5. It has 5 plus 5 minus 1 red tiles, which is 9. Count them and see!
Some numbers are the sum of two perfect squares. For example, 13 is 4 plus 9. One of these 4 numbers is not.

board.text: Which is NOT a sum of two perfect squares?

beats.say: The squares small enough to use are 1, 4, 9, 16 and 25.
Test 20. Take away 4, and 16 is left. Both are squares, so 20 can be made.
Test 34. Take away 25. What is left, and is it a square?

choices: 9, but it is not a square
ask.ifNot: 34 minus 25 is 9, and 9 is 3 times 3. So 34 is 25 plus 9, which is two squares.

beats.say: 34 is 9 plus 25. And 29 is 4 plus 25. Both can be made.
Now 21. Take away each square in turn: 20, 17, 12 and 5 are left. None of those is a square.
So 21 cannot be made.
The method: take away one square, and see whether a square is left. Try every square, so that nothing is missed.
Soldiers stand in a square. Then 3 full rows and 3 full columns march away, 69 soldiers in all, and a smaller square is left.

board.text: Square of soldiers. 3 rows and 3 columns leave: 69 go.

beats.say: When 3 rows and 3 columns leave, the square that remains has sides that are 3 shorter.
Is 69 simply 3 rows plus 3 columns of soldiers?

choices: No, some soldiers are in both
ask.ifNot: A soldier in the corner is in a row that leaves and also in a column that leaves. He must not be counted twice.

beats.say: That is the trap, so we go a safer way. The soldiers who left are the big square minus the small square.
Test sides of 12 and 9. 144 minus 81 is 63. Not enough.
Test sides of 13 and 10. 169 minus 100 is 69. That matches!
So at first there were 13 rows of 13, which is 169 soldiers.
Careful: 69 divided by 3 is 23, but a 23 by 23 square would lose far more than 69 soldiers.
In each pair the two numbers add up to 60. Which pair has the greatest product? We can find out without doing all four.
Learn from small numbers first. Take pairs that add up to 10.
5 times 5 is 25, 4 times 6 is 24 and 3 times 7 is 21. What happens as the two numbers move apart?

ask.ifNot: 25, then 24, then 21. The further apart the two numbers are, the smaller the product.

beats.say: The equal pair wins. The further apart the numbers move, the smaller the product gets.
The same happens here. The equal pair is 30 times 30, which is 900.
29 times 31 is 899, just 1 less. And 28 times 32 is 896.
So the greatest product is 30 times 30.
Careful: 33 is the biggest number here, but its partner 27 is the smallest. For the same sum, the square always wins.
Look at the pattern in the question. We use it to find 11111 times 11111 without multiplying.
121. 12321. 1234321. The digits climb up, and then come back down.
11 has two 1s, and its answer climbs to 2. 111 has three 1s, and its answer climbs to 3. How high will 11111 climb?

ask.ifNot: Count the 1s in 11111. There are 5 of them, so the answer climbs to 5.

beats.say: 11111 has five 1s. So the answer climbs to 5 and comes back down.
Now add its digits. Going up: 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5 make 15.
Coming down: 4, 3, 2 and 1 make 10.
15 plus 10 is 25.
The trap is to stop at 15. The digits come back down too. And look: 25 is 5 times 5, another square!
Kabir's age is a perfect square now. In 9 years it will be a perfect square again. How old is he?

board.text: Age now: a perfect square. In 9 years: a square again.

beats.say: List some perfect squares that could be ages.
Add 9 to each, and see if we land on another square. 1 becomes 10. 4 becomes 13. 9 becomes 18. No luck yet.
Now try 16. What is 16 plus 9, and is it a square?

choices: 25, but it is not a square
ask.ifNot: 16 plus 9 is 25. And 25 is 5 times 5, so it is a perfect square.

beats.say: 16 plus 9 is 25, which is 5 times 5. It works!
Could a bigger age work too? 25 plus 9 is 34. 36 plus 9 is 45. No. After 16, the squares are more than 9 apart.
So Kabir is 16 this year.
Careful: 25 is the age he will reach, not his age now.
We multiply 12 by something to get a perfect square. But the square must be greater than 100. We want the smallest multiplier.
First, what turns 12 into any perfect square? 12 is 2 times 2 times 3. The 3 has no partner.
Multiply by 3, and we get 36, a perfect square. But look at the question again.
36 is a perfect square. Does it answer the question?

choices: No, it is not greater than 100
ask.ifNot: The question wants a perfect square greater than 100. 36 is far below 100.

beats.say: This is the trap. 36 is too small. So we look at bigger multipliers, for a square above 100.
12 times 9 is 108. That is above 100, but 108 is between 100 and 121, so it is not a square.
12 times 12 is 144. A perfect square, and greater than 100!
And nothing smaller works. The only square between 100 and 144 is 121, and 12 does not divide 121.
Anu squares an odd number and subtracts 1. Some number always divides her answer. We want the greatest such number.
Try the first few odd numbers. 3 squared is 9, and 9 minus 1 is 8.
5 squared is 25, minus 1 is 24. 7 squared is 49, minus 1 is 48. 9 squared is 81, minus 1 is 80.
The very first answer is 8. Can a number bigger than 8 divide 8 exactly?

ask.ifNot: A number cannot be divided exactly by something bigger than itself. So nothing above 8 can divide every answer.

beats.say: This is the key idea. The first answer is 8, so our number cannot be more than 8. That rules out 16 and 24.
Does 8 divide them all? 24 is 3 times 8. 48 is 6 times 8. 80 is 10 times 8. Yes!
So the greatest number that always divides her answer is 8.
Careful: 4 divides them all too, but it is not the greatest. And 24 divides some of the answers, but not all.
The year 2025 is 45 times 45, a perfect square. How many years until the next perfect square year?

board.text: 2025 = 45 × 45. Years until the next perfect square = ?

beats.say: Which multiplication gives the next perfect square?

ask.ifNot: Perfect squares come from the counting numbers, one after another. After 45 times 45 comes 46 times 46.

beats.say: The next square is 46 times 46. Build it up. 46 times 45 is one more 45 than 45 times 45. That is 2070.
Then 46 times 46 is one more 46. 2070 plus 46 is 2116.
So the next perfect square year is 2116. That is 91 years after 2025.
Notice: we added 45 and then 46, and 45 plus 46 is 91. Neighbouring squares always differ by the sum of the two numbers.
Careful: 90 is twice 45, which is 1 short. And 46 is the next number to square, not the number of years.
The hall has as many rows as there are chairs in each row, and every chair is filled. Which of these could be the number of men?

board.text: Rows = chairs in each row. How many men?

beats.say: Think of a small hall: 5 rows of 5 chairs hold 25 men. So what kind of number is the number of men?

ask.ifNot: Men equals rows times chairs in a row, and those two are the same. So it is a number times itself: a square number.

beats.say: So we are looking for a square number. Let us test each choice against squares we know.
131: 11 times 11 is 121 and 12 times 12 is 144. 131 falls in between, so it is not a square.
275: 16 times 16 is 256 and 17 times 17 is 289. In between again, so not a square.
Now try 18. 18 times 18 is 324. That is one of our choices!
Careful with 325. It is only 1 more than 324, but a full hall needs an exact square. One extra man would have no chair.
So the number of men can be 324.
So: equal rows and columns means a square number. Test each choice by squeezing it between two squares.
For each pair, we square both numbers and add. We want a total that is itself a square number.

board.text: Sum of the squares of which two is a square?

beats.say: 2 and 3: the squares are 4 and 9, and together they make 13. Not a square.
5 and 6: 25 plus 36 is 61. And 4 and 6: 16 plus 36 is 52.
7 times 7 is 49 and 8 times 8 is 64. So are 52 and 61 squares?

ask.ifNot: 52 and 61 are both more than 49 and less than 64. No whole number lies between 7 and 8, so neither is a square.

beats.say: Now 6 and 8: 36 plus 64 is 100.
And 100 is 10 times 10. A square! So the pair is 6 and 8.
Notice: 6, 8 and 10 are the famous 3, 4 and 5, doubled. 9 plus 16 is 25 as well.
We count the square numbers that have 2 digits and are even.
First list every 2-digit square. Start at 4 times 4, which is 16, and stop before 10 times 10, which is 100.
Which numbers give an even square?

ask.ifNot: Even times even is even, and odd times odd is odd. So only even numbers give even squares.

beats.say: Even times even is even. So the even squares come from 4, 6 and 8.
That is 16, 36 and 64. So there are 3 of them.
Careful: 6 is the count of all the 2-digit squares. The question wants only the even ones.
And 4 and 100 are even squares too, but they do not have 2 digits.
4 pairs of numbers. We add each pair, and look for a total that is a square number.

board.text: Which pair adds up to a square number?

beats.say: First pair: 91 plus 19 is 110.
Is 110 a square number? 10 times 10 is 100 and 11 times 11 is 121.

choices: No, it falls between two squares
ask.ifNot: 110 is more than 100 but less than 121. There is no whole number between 10 and 11, so 110 is not a square.

beats.say: 110 sits between 100 and 121, so it is not a square. Next pair: 157 plus 68 is 225.
225 is 15 times 15. A square number!
Let us check the others, to be sure. 59 plus 52 is 111, and 76 plus 78 is 154. Neither is a square.
So the pair is 157 and 68.
A tip: learn the squares of the numbers up to 15 by heart. Then you spot 225 at once.
We add something to 710 to reach a square number. So we need the first square above 710.

spec.note: How far is the next square?

beats.say: Where to start? 25 times 25 is 625, too small. 30 times 30 is 900, too big.
Try 26. 26 times 26 is 676. Still below 710.
676 is still below 710. What should we try next?

ask.ifNot: We need a square above 710, so we go up one more, to 27 times 27.

beats.say: 27 times 27: 27 times 20 is 540 and 27 times 7 is 189. Together, 729. That is above 710!
The gap from 710 up to 729 is 19.
Check: 710 plus 19 is 729, which is 27 times 27.
Careful: landing near 729 is not enough. A square has to be hit exactly.
We want the square root of 576. That means: which number, times itself, makes 576?
20 times 20 is 400, and 30 times 30 is 900. Our 576 lies in between, so the answer is between 20 and 30.
Now a clever clue. 576 ends in 6. Which last digit gives a square that ends in 6?

ask.ifNot: Square each digit and look at the last digit of the result. Only 4 or 6 gives a square that ends in 6.

beats.say: 4 times 4 is 16. 6 times 6 is 36. Both end in 6. So we try 24 or 26.
Try 24. 24 times 20 is 480, and 24 times 4 is 96. Together that is 576. That is our number!
So the square root of 576 is 24.
Careful: a square root is not a half. Half of 576 is 288. But 288 times just 2 is already 576, so 288 times itself is far too big.
So remember: a square root undoes squaring. Ask yourself which number, times itself, gives 576.
The square root of 16 is the number that, multiplied by itself, gives 16. Let us hunt for it.
Let us try a number. 3 times 3 is 9. That is too small.
So try the next number, 4. What is 4 times 4?

ask.ifNot: 4 times 4 means 4 lots of 4, and that makes 16. Adding 4 and 4 gives only 8.

beats.say: 4 times 4 is 16. That is exactly our number!
So the square root of 16 is 4.
Careful: a square root is not a half. Half of 16 is 8, and 8 times 8 is far too big.
So remember: a square root undoes squaring. Ask yourself which number, times itself, gives 16.
We want the square of 23. Squaring a number means multiplying it by itself.
So which sum is the square of 23?

ask.ifNot: Squaring means multiplying a number by itself. So the square of 23 is 23 times 23.

beats.say: 23 times 23 is a big sum, so split the second 23 into 20 and 3.
23 times 20 is 460.
23 times 3 is 69.
Add the two parts. 460 plus 69 is 529.
A quick check on the last digit: 3 times 3 is 9, so the square must end in 9. It does.
Careful: 46 is just 23 doubled. Squaring is times itself, and that grows much faster.
